clinicalPearls: A rare non-hereditary syndrome defined by the association of gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumours, paragangliomas, and pulmonary chondromas
It overwhelmingly affects young women and is distinct from the autosomal dominant Carney-Stratakis dyad of GIST and paraganglioma
The gastric stromal tumours are typically multifocal, wild-type for KIT and PDGFRA, and characterised by loss of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity
Patients rarely have all three components at once; two of the three, or one plus another related tumour, may fulfil the diagnosis over time
Additional associated lesions include phaeochromocytoma, oesophageal leiomyoma, and adrenocortical adenoma
Management is tumour-directed surgery with lifelong surveillance, as the SDH-deficient GISTs behave differently from conventional GISTs and often respond poorly to standard tyrosine kinase inhibitors
Consider Carney triad in a young woman with a wild-type, SDH-deficient gastric GIST, and screen for paraganglioma and pulmonary chondroma
reference.pathophysiology: Carney triad is associated with deficient function of the succinate dehydrogenase enzyme complex, most often through epigenetic silencing (such as hypermethylation of the SDHC promoter) rather than germline mutation, which is why the condition is generally not inherited. Loss of succinate dehydrogenase impairs mitochondrial energy metabolism and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors, promoting a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic state that drives tumour formation. This mechanism underlies the SDH-deficient gastric stromal tumours, the paragangliomas and phaeochromocytomas, and the other component lesions. Because the SDH-deficient GISTs differ molecularly from KIT- or PDGFRA-driven tumours, they follow an indolent but persistent course and respond less predictably to conventional targeted therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Carney-Stratakis syndrome (dyad of GIST and paraganglioma)
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen for gastric stromal tumours
Biochemical screening for catecholamine excess (plasma or urinary metanephrines)
Functional and anatomical imaging to localise paragangliomas
Immunohistochemistry for SDHB loss on tumour tissue
Molecular testing to distinguish SDH-deficient from KIT/PDGFRA-mutant tumours
redFlags: Gastrointestinal bleeding or anaemia from a gastric stromal tumour
Paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, or sweating from a catecholamine-secreting tumour
Metastatic spread of an SDH-deficient GIST
New or enlarging masses on surveillance imaging
reference.prognosis: The SDH-deficient gastric tumours are frequently multifocal and can metastasise, yet often follow a protracted indolent course, so long-term survival can be favourable with surgery and surveillance despite recurrent disease; paraganglioma-related morbidity depends on catecholamine excess and tumour location.
pitfalls: Treating an SDH-deficient GIST like a conventional GIST and expecting a good response to standard tyrosine kinase inhibitors
Missing an occult catecholamine-secreting tumour before surgery
Failing to recognise that the full triad rarely presents simultaneously
Confusing the non-hereditary triad with the inherited Carney-Stratakis dyad
management: Manage the gastric stromal tumours with tumour-directed surgical resection, preserving stomach where possible given their multifocal, indolent nature
Resect functioning paragangliomas and phaeochromocytomas with preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade for catecholamine excess
Monitor pulmonary chondromas and resect only where diagnostically or symptomatically necessary
Recognise the poor response of these succinate dehydrogenase-deficient tumours to conventional tyrosine kinase inhibitors when planning therapy
Maintain lifelong surveillance with abdominal, chest and functional imaging and biochemical screening, as components accrue over time
Coordinate multidisciplinary surgical, oncology and endocrine care, with genetic assessment to distinguish the non-hereditary triad from germline SDHx syndromes
